title: Learning and the Hedgehog - 1
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton borrows Jim Collins' Hedgehog Concept, the single simple idea that organisations use as a frame of reference for every decision, and argues that learning should play that role in schools. He uses the comedian analogy, where laughter is the point and rapport and timing are merely factors that affect laughter, to show how education confuses learning with the factors around it. He claims that many schools slip into other priorities, often nudged by governments. His evidence is anecdotal but striking: no one at an 800-person conference had worked in a school with a shared definition of learning, few staff meetings discuss learning, and classroom visits usually give feedback on teaching rather than learning. He concludes that teaching is an important factor but is not itself learning, and he invites readers to audit their own schools against these three tests.
points: Learning should be the single simple idea that frames every school decision, and organisations cannot focus relentlessly on several competing ideas.
The comedian analogy separates the heart of the game (laughter, learning) from supporting factors (timing, teaching) that are easy to mistake for it.
Skelton's three diagnostics are a shared definition of learning, time given to learning at staff meetings, and classroom visits that look at learning rather than teaching.
Observing a teacher teach is not evidence that students learn, just as watching a chef does not show the food tastes good.
Schools often lack the focus through no fault of their own, having drifted under outside pressure rather than through obstruction.
quotes: When they are on stage, comedians will do anything and change anything to get laughs. Laughter is the very simple concept that is used by comedians as a frame of reference for all their decisions.

In education, we often confuse learning (the heart of the game) with the factors that affect learning (the supporting things that are super helpful but aren’t the central focus). We spend way too much time talking about, legislating for, and being judged on the factors that affect learning before we talk about learning itself. It’s back to front We are all suffering because of it; especially our children and students.
But many schools don’t have learning as their hedgehog concept. It's not because they are being obstructive or deliberately perverse.
I ask how many of them have ever worked in a school which had a shared definition of learning. The answer? None.
Teaching is a factor that affects learning, an important factor. But it isn’t learning.

How we can help schools become schools that have learning at their centre is the driver behind all of these posts. It’s essentially what the second part of my career has been about and why I am writing this now.
